items.title: Counting the bottles: what a refill station actually saves
items.excerpt: A single refill programme on a busy site replaces six figures of plastic bottles a year. Here is the arithmetic, the assumptions behind it, and how to turn it into numbers your sustainability report can use.
items.cover_alt: A stainless steel drinking fountain beside a running track in a Gulf city park at sunset
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Every sustainability report I read has the same problem. Lots of ambition, very few numbers. Refill stations are one of the rare places where the numbers are simple, provable and big enough to matter.

So here is the arithmetic, with every assumption on the table.

## The basic sum

Bottles avoided in a year is people on site, times refills per person per day, times days the site is open.

Take an office or school with 600 people, each refilling once a day, open on weekdays only, about 250 days a year.

600 × 1 × 250 = **150,000 bottles a year.**

That is one refill each. Most people refill more than once on a hot day, so treat it as a floor, not a ceiling.

## Turning bottles into plastic, carbon and money

These are the planning assumptions we use in the calculator on our homepage. They are estimates, not certified figures, and you should swap in your own if you have them.

| Assumption | Value we use |
| --- | --- |
| PET in a 500 ml bottle | 10 g |
| Carbon per bottle, production to disposal | 80 g CO₂e |
| Price per bottle | AED 1.00 |

On 150,000 bottles that comes to:

- **1.5 tonnes** of PET plastic that never gets made, shipped or thrown away
- **12 tonnes** of CO₂e avoided
- **AED 150,000** of bottled water spend replaced

Double the refills to two a day and every number doubles. Open seven days a week, as a hospital, airport or mall does, and multiply by 365 instead of 250.

## Why this matters for reporting

Most frameworks your clients report against, whether that is Estidama, LEED or a corporate ESG target, reward reducing waste and water consumption. A refill programme gives you a measurable number to put against those goals, which is more than most initiatives can claim. Check which credits or targets your project is actually going for. The frameworks change, and the specific credit matters more than the headline.

Two things make the number credible.

**Measure it.** Many bottle filling stations have a counter that shows bottles saved. Specify units with a counter and you replace an estimate with a real figure.

**Make it easy.** Usage follows convenience. Put refill stations where people already walk, chill the water, and make sure there is no queue. A unit tucked behind a stairwell does not move the number.

## Where the savings are biggest

The sites with the most people per day win: airports, metro stations, universities, large schools, hospitals and stadiums. For a stadium, the per event number is the one to report, because a full house refilling once is tens of thousands of bottles in a single afternoon.

## Run your own numbers

Our impact calculator does this sum for any site in a few seconds and shows the assumptions underneath it. Put in your head count, refills and opening days, and use the result in your business case.

If you want help sizing a refill programme for a specific site, send the floor plan and the occupancy. We will come back with the number of stations, where to put them and a priced quote within one working day.

items.title: ANSI Z358.1 in plain English: the eyewash and shower checks that fail audits
items.excerpt: Most emergency showers in the Gulf were compliant on the day they were installed. The audit fails come later, and they are nearly always the same five things. Here they are, with the numbers that matter.
items.cover_alt: A green combination safety shower and eyewash station on a grated floor in a process plant
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
I grew Hughes Safety Showers from £3.9M to £6.9M, so I have seen a lot of emergency equipment in a lot of plants. What strikes me every time is this. Almost every unit was compliant the day it went in. The failures come afterwards, and they come from the same short list.

[ANSI/ISEA Z358.1](https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/) is the American national standard for emergency eyewash and shower equipment, and it is the one I see specified most often. EN 15154 is the European series, with separate parts for [laboratory body showers](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025) and [plumbed in eyewash units](https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025), so check which part your project names. This is the plain English version of what the American standard asks for, and where sites fall down. The equipment itself sits in our [Emergency division](https://aquelon.com/divisions/emergency/).

## The numbers that matter

The full standard is a paid document from its publisher. These figures are as set out, with section numbers, in [Bradley's quick compliance guide to Z358.1](https://www.webstaurantstore.com/documents/pdf/4055_efx_quick_compliance_guide.pdf).

| Requirement | What Z358.1 asks for |
| --- | --- |
| Reach | Within 10 seconds of the hazard, roughly 17 metres, on the same level |
| Activation | Valve opens in one second or less and stays open without hands |
| Eyewash flow | At least 1.5 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Shower flow | At least 75.7 litres per minute for a full 15 minutes |
| Water temperature | Tepid, between 16°C and 38°C |
| Shower head height | Between 208 cm and 244 cm above the floor |
| Spray pattern | At least 50.8 cm across at 152 cm above the floor |
| Weekly check | Activate every unit to clear the line and confirm flow |
| Annual check | Full inspection against the standard |

Those numbers are the easy part. Keeping a site inside them is the hard part.

## Fail one: the water is too hot

This is the big one in the Gulf. [The standard says tepid](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/), which means no hotter than 38°C. An exposed supply line in a Jubail or Ruwais summer will deliver water well above that for the first minutes of flow. Tepid is there for a reason: [the guide to the standard](https://www.webstaurantstore.com/documents/pdf/4055_efx_quick_compliance_guide.pdf) says it is to encourage the injured person to keep flushing for the full 15 minutes.

The fix is designed in, not bolted on. Specify a tempered water system: a chiller, a [thermostatic mixing valve](https://aquelon.com/products/acorn-et71-1-bvs-otg/), or a [tank shower with a chiller option](https://aquelon.com/products/hughes-exp-j-14ks-1500/). Insulate and shade the supply line. Then test the temperature at the outlet in July, not in January.

## Fail two: something is in the way

The route to the unit has to be clear and on the same level. Ten seconds is not long. On audit day it is common to find a pallet, a hose reel or a new piece of plant parked in front of the shower, or a unit that now sits behind a door that was added after commissioning.

Walk the route from each hazard, time it, and repeat it every time the layout changes.

## Fail three: nobody runs it weekly

The weekly activation does two jobs. It proves nothing is blocking the flow, and it clears the stagnant water sitting in the pipe, which [the guide to the standard](https://www.webstaurantstore.com/documents/pdf/4055_efx_quick_compliance_guide.pdf) names as a contamination risk. That standing water is what the injured worker gets first.

Weekly checks get skipped because they are boring and nobody owns them. Put a named person against every unit, and log it. This is exactly why we built [Z358 One](https://z358one.com/): so the weekly and annual checks are recorded, timestamped and visible to the safety team, instead of living on a clipboard.

## Fail four: flow is below the minimum

Pressure drops as a site grows. A shower that delivered 76 litres per minute at commissioning can fall below the line once new users are added to the same main. Eyewash nozzles also scale up and partially block, especially with hard water.

Measure flow at the annual inspection with a proper gauge or a calibrated bucket. Do not eyeball it. Fit dust covers on eyewash heads and clean the nozzles as part of the weekly check.

## Fail five: you cannot see it

The unit has to be identified with a highly visible sign and the area has to be well lit. Signs fade in UV, get painted over during shutdowns and get hidden by new cabling. A worker with chemicals in their eyes is not reading small print. Check the signage and lighting at every annual inspection.

## What to put in the specification

If you are writing a spec for a new facility, ask for:

- Units certified to ANSI Z358.1 or EN 15154 by the manufacturer, with test data
- A tempered water solution sized for 15 minutes of full flow at peak summer supply temperature
- Freeze protection only where it is genuinely needed. Heat is the Gulf problem
- Stainless or coated finishes suited to the chemicals on site
- Flow and temperature test results at commissioning, recorded per unit
- Data sheets and certificates for the submittal pack, which is what our [technical library](https://aquelon.com/library/) is for
- A weekly and annual inspection regime handed over with the equipment

## The short version

Compliant on day one is not the same as compliant on audit day. Control the temperature. Keep the route clear. Run every unit every week. Measure flow once a year. Make sure people can see it.

If you are specifying or replacing emergency equipment, [send the layout and the hazard list](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with compliant units, a tempered water option and pricing within one working day.

## Sources

- International Safety Equipment Association, "American National Standard for Emergency Eyewash and Shower Equipment", ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014. https://safetyequipment.org/worker_protections/emergency-eyewash-shower/
- Bradley Corporation, "ANSI/ISEA Z358.1-2014 Quick Compliance Guide". https://www.webstaurantstore.com/documents/pdf/4055_efx_quick_compliance_guide.pdf
- American National Standards Institute, "ANSI Z358.1-2014: Emergency Eyewash and Shower Standard". https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-z358-1-emergency-eyewash-station-shower/
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-1:2025, Plumbed-in body showers for laboratories", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-1-2025
- Estonian Centre for Standardisation, "EVS-EN 15154-2:2025, Plumbed-in eyewash units", 2025. https://www.evs.ee/en/evs-en-15154-2-2025

items.title: Specifying drinking fountains for GCC schools: what to put in the tender
items.excerpt: A school fountain in the Gulf has to survive 45°C, salt air and a thousand pupils a day. Here is what I would write into the specification so the units you approve are the units that still work in year five.
items.cover_alt: Two pupils drinking from stainless steel pedestal fountains under a shade canopy in a school courtyard
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
A drinking fountain looks like the simplest line on a school BOQ. It is usually the one that comes back to bite the contractor. Units get specified off a European catalogue, installed in full sun, and by the second summer the water is warm, the bubblers are blocked and the facilities team is raising tickets.

I have spent thirty years selling equipment into projects. The pattern is always the same. The problems are written in at specification stage, not on site. So here is what I would put in the tender for a [school in the GCC](https://aquelon.com/sectors/education/).

## Start with the number of units, not the model

Decide how many outlets the site needs before anyone picks a product. Table 403.1 of the International Plumbing Code is the usual starting point, at one drinking fountain per 100 occupants for educational buildings, as shown in [this published state adoption of the table](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/regs/5416.docx). Check what your authority actually adopts, because it varies by emirate and by country.

Then think about where pupils are, not just how many. Break times put the whole school in one courtyard for twenty minutes. Two fountains at the far end of a corridor meet the ratio and still leave a queue. Put outlets where the crowds form: playgrounds, sports halls, canteens and the main circulation routes.

## Write the climate into the specification

This is where most specifications fall short. A unit that performs in Warsaw or Ohio is not automatically fit for a Riyadh playground in August.

- **Chilled water where pupils actually drink.** Outdoor pipework in direct sun heats the water standing in it, and children will not drink warm water. Specify a chiller or a [chilled bottle filler](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-mgym74-a021/) for the main outlets, and shade the unit where you can.
- **Stainless steel grade.** AISI 304 is fine inland. Near the sea, specify AISI 316, which has [better resistance to pitting in chloride environments](https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up), or a powder coated finish rated for coastal exposure.
- **Powder coat to a RAL reference.** If the architect wants colour, write the RAL number into the spec and ask for a physical sample before approval. Screen colours lie.

## Design for heavy use and abuse

Schools are hard on equipment. Pupils hang off fountains, push things into bubblers and press buttons a hundred times a minute for fun.

- Vandal resistant bubblers with a protective guard, so mouths never touch the outlet.
- Push buttons that are mechanical and self closing, or sensor operation if the budget allows. Avoid twist taps.
- Fixings that cannot be undone with a coin or a ruler.
- Units bolted to a proper base or wall, not just sealed to the floor.

## Make it accessible

Specify at least one accessible outlet at every location. A [dual height unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-grm45/) covers both: a lower bowl for younger pupils and wheelchair users, a standard height bowl for older pupils and staff. Ask for the clear knee space and the reach range to be shown on the datasheet. [Section 602 of the ADA Standards](https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602) is the benchmark I see consultants use most.

## Bottle fillers are now the default

Most schools I see now want pupils carrying reusable bottles. A bottle filling station handles that far better than a bubbler. It fills a bottle quickly, it is easier to keep hygienic, and [some units count bottles saved](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-bf16s/), which head teachers like to report.

The best answer for a school is usually a [combination unit](https://aquelon.com/products/murdock-gym74/): bubbler and bottle filler on one pedestal. You get both behaviours from one water connection and one drain.

## Plan the water quality

A fountain is only as good as what comes into it. Specify an inline filter at each unit, sized for the expected flow, and put filter changes on the maintenance schedule from day one. Write in who changes them and how often. If nobody owns the filter, nobody changes it.

## What the submittal pack should include

Ask every bidder for the same pack so you compare like with like. Our [technical library](https://aquelon.com/library/) shows what ours contains:

- Product datasheet with dimensions, flow rates, materials and connections
- CE certificate and the manufacturer's ISO quality certificate
- Hygiene or drinking water approval for the materials in contact with water
- Installation guide with the fixing and plumbing details
- Warranty terms and the local service arrangement
- Lead time to site, by model

If a bidder cannot produce these quickly, that tells you something about the support you will get in year three.

## The short version

Count outlets by where pupils gather. Chill the water. Match the steel to the site. Specify for abuse. Make every location accessible. Put bottle fillers in as standard. Own the filters.

Get those right in the tender and the fountains stop being the line that bites you.

If you are writing a school specification now, [send me the scope](https://aquelon.com/quote/). We will come back with compliant models, pricing and the submittal pack within one working day.

## Sources

- South Carolina Building Codes Council, "Document 5416, International Plumbing Code amendments, minimum plumbing facilities table". https://www.scstatehouse.gov/regs/5416.docx
- US Access Board, "ADA Accessibility Standards, section 602 Drinking Fountains". https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-602
- Australian Stainless Steel Development Association, "316: The First Step Up". https://www.assda.asn.au/stainless-steel/grade-selection/316-the-first-step-up
